rawItems.title: Crews rush to 'deliberate' fire at former RAF base in Hunts village
rawItems.content: Firefighters rushed to a "deliberate" fire at a derelict former RAF base in a Huntingdonshire village. Crews were called to the former RAF Upwood site on Ramsey Road near Bury on Saturday, November 21, at 3.31pm. The base opened in 1917 after a nearby farm was requisitioned for use as an emergency landing ground. Standing mostly derelict since 1994, the site has been the target of fly tipping and arson attacks for a number of years. However, there have been plans to redevelop areas into community facilities. Crews from Ramsey arrived to find a blaze on the ground floor of the derelict building and used a hose reel to extinguish it. They returned to the station by 4.10pm. A statement from Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service reads: "The cause of the fire is believed to be deliberate." Anyone with information should contact Cambridgeshire Police via their website, quoting incident 445 of November 21. Alternatively, call Crimestoppers on 0800 555111.

"Bloom and Brew will operate as a family-friendly café and restaurant. rawItems.content: Autumn 2026 Ramsey Town Council Residents Communication RAMSEY COMMUNITIES NEIGHBOURHOOD PLAN A further step forward The Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan has been prepared with local voices at the heart. People gave their opinions via consultation over the summer of 2025 and the plan was then put together by a steering group of residents before going back out as a draft for further consultation. The next major step will be a community vote through a referendum organised by Huntingdonshire District Council, likely to be in December 2026. It will be organised in the same way as an election and everyone on the electoral register will be notified. You will be asked whether you accept the Neighbourhood Plan - yes or no. We will produce a quick reference guide for anyone who may not have time to read the full document. Key points include: Providing new infrastructure, facilities and services so new development benefits existing, new and future residents. Supporting a vibrant community with places to live, work, stay and play, including affordable housing and housing with a local connection. Protecting the historic environment, heritage assets and green spaces that matter to the community. Having our Neighbourhood Plan in place will mean Ramsey receives 25% of developer contributions rather than the current 15%. That means more money can be spent directly in our community. neighbourhood.plan@ramseytowncouncil.gov.uk

rawItems.content: CIL - Community Infrastructure Levy What is CIL? Community Infrastructure Levy, commonly referred to as CIL, is money collected by Huntingdonshire District Council from certain new developments. The funding is then used to help provide or improve infrastructure needed as communities grow. The money collected is broadly divided into three areas: Up to 5% can be retained by Huntingdonshire District Council towards the administration and collection of CIL. 15% is normally allocated to the Town or Parish Council for the area where the development takes place. Once an adopted Neighbourhood Plan is in place, this increases to 25%. Most of the remaining funding is retained by Huntingdonshire District Council for larger strategic infrastructure projects across the district. Ramsey Town Council currently receives the 15% neighbourhood portion. Once the Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan is adopted, this will increase to 25%, giving the Council a greater share of money from qualifying development to invest back into our communities. Current projects supported or earmarked through Ramsey Town Council’s CIL funding include: Improvements at The Moorings. Contributions towards Local Highways Improvement projects. Improvements to Newtown Road Play Park. Improvements to the public toilets. New benches at the skate park. CCTV at The Moorings and New Road. The Double Yellow Lines project. The Town Council is also considering future projects, including additional parking behind the doctor’s surgery at Mews Close. Local Highways Initiative Bid (LHI): what is an LHI? The Local Highway Improvement programme allows local councils and community organisations to apply to Cambridgeshire County Council for funding towards highway improvements. Projects can include new or extended footpaths, traffic-calming measures, speed-reduction schemes, and other changes designed to improve road and pedestrian safety. Ramsey Town Council identifies potential projects and submits applications to Cambridgeshire County Council. Applications are assessed by the County Council and, if successful, funding is awarded towards the cost of the scheme. Under the current scheme, up to £25,000 can be awarded towards more complex projects, with applicants expected to contribute at least 10% of the overall cost. One recent LHI project was the extension of the footpath along Stocking Fen Road towards the industrial estate, improving pedestrian access for people travelling to and from work. The Council has also submitted an application for speed-reduction measures on the approach to Ramsey St Mary’s and is awaiting the outcome. Abbey College Road Safety Campaign Abbey College students are raising funds towards the £10,000 needed to help pay for speed reduction measures on Hollow Lane. Students have been campaigning, the school submitted an LHI bid, and speed cushions are planned. They would be grateful if you could spare the price of a coffee and scan the QR code.

rawItems.meetingTitle: Ramsey Town Council Residents Communication – Autumn 2026
rawItems.content: Message from the Mayor of Ramsey Hello everyone, I hope you’ve all had a wonderful summer. Personally, I can’t believe how quickly this year has flown by and that, as I write this, we’re already going into autumn. I want to use this column to recognise some amazing people - the Ramsey Town Council staff team, led by our Clerk, Lisa Renfree. They have had an incredibly busy summer, with lots of change and new initiatives to contend with as our Council grows and new Councillors come on board with the ambition to achieve and deliver more for our residents. They organised the Bands on the Green programme, delivered a family fun day at QEII Park with entertainment from the Blues Brothers and Queen tribute acts, produced and managed delivery of our newsletters to 5,000 homes, and got to grips with a new finance system. This was all on top of day-to- day customer service and administration, room bookings, council meetings and communications. They also stepped up to help coordinate meals and drinks for firefighters at Holme Fen during the recent wildfire, when the RRT Charity had to leave after a week. They do all of this professionally and with a smile. More often, however, they are facing abusive behaviour and, as a Council, this is something we will not tolerate. We have had to notify the police and use CCTV as evidence. Thankfully, this behaviour comes from a minority, and I know many of you appreciate the time our staff takes to assist you. So, from me and all fellow Councillors: thank you Lisa, Amanda, Kay, Alison, Quincy, Morgan and Paul - you are appreciated. Keep up the great work for our community. Thank you, Ramsey Parish community and beyond On behalf of Ramsey Town Council, we would like to thank everyone who supported the firefighters responding to the fire at Holme Fen. The response from local businesses, organisations and volunteers was incredible. Our thanks go to The Farmers Coffee Shop, Gorilla Pizza and Friar Tuck Fish & Chips for providing food and support; Ramsey Community Centre for opening its kitchen to prepare the large quantity of meals needed; The Admiral Wells for becoming a hub of activity, preparing meals and acting as a donation drop-off point; and Stevelyn & Creative Crafters for also providing a collection point, to name just a few. We would also like to thank the many volunteers who gave their time to prepare food and help wherever needed, as well as everyone who made donations. The JustGiving appeal raised an amazing £4,546.56. The Mayor also had the privilege of meeting The Duke of Gloucester during his visit to Holme Fen, where he saw the devastation caused by the fire and personally thanked firefighters, the owners of The Admiral Wells and local volunteers for their incredible efforts. The Lord-Lieutenant, Julie Spence, who accompanied him, spoke of how proud she was to see the community come together so quickly and effectively. Firefighters expressed their appreciation for every meal, drink and homemade cake provided during the response. Following the fire, a meeting of local community groups has been arranged for 1 October to discuss emergency planning and how the community can work together in response to future major incidents.

rawItems.content: Autumn 2026 Ramsey Town Council Residents Communication RAMSEY COMMUNITIES NEIGHBOURHOOD PLAN A further step forward The Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan has been prepared with local voices at the heart. People gave their opinions via consultation over the summer of 2025 and the plan was then put together by a steering group of residents before going back out as a draft for further consultation. We’re pleased to say that it has also passed another significant step - Independent Assessment. Further details can be found on the Ramsey Town Council website. What happens next? The next major step will be a community vote through a referendum organised by Huntingdonshire District Council, likely to be in December 2026. It will be organised in the same way as an election and everyone on the electoral register will be notified. You will be asked whether you accept the Neighbourhood Plan - yes or no. We will produce a quick reference guide for anyone who may not have time to read the full document. Key points include: Providing new infrastructure, facilities and services so new development benefits existing, new and future residents. Supporting a vibrant community with places to live, work, stay and play, including affordable housing and housing with a local connection. Protecting the historic environment, heritage assets and green spaces that matter to the community. Having our Neighbourhood Plan in place will mean Ramsey receives 25% of developer contributions rather than the current 15%. That means more money can be spent directly in our community. neighbourhood.plan@ramseytowncouncil.gov.uk

rawItems.content: CIL - Community Infrastructure Levy What is CIL? Community Infrastructure Levy, commonly referred to as CIL, is money collected by Huntingdonshire District Council from certain new developments. The funding is then used to help provide or improve infrastructure needed as communities grow. The money collected is broadly divided into three areas: Up to 5% can be retained by Huntingdonshire District Council towards the administration and collection of CIL. 15% is normally allocated to the Town or Parish Council for the area where the development takes place. Once an adopted Neighbourhood Plan is in place, this increases to 25%. Most of the remaining funding is retained by Huntingdonshire District Council for larger strategic infrastructure projects across the district. Ramsey Town Council currently receives the 15% neighbourhood portion. Once the Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan is adopted, this will increase to 25%, giving the Council a greater share of money from qualifying development to invest back into our communities. Current projects supported or earmarked through Ramsey Town Council’s CIL funding include: Improvements at The Moorings. Contributions towards Local Highways Improvement projects. Improvements to Newtown Road Play Park. Improvements to the public toilets. New benches at the skate park. CCTV at The Moorings and New Road. The Double Yellow Lines project. The Town Council is also considering future projects, including additional parking behind the doctor’s surgery at Mews Close. Local Highways Initiative Bid (LHI): what is an LHI? The Local Highway Improvement programme allows local councils and community organisations to apply to Cambridgeshire County Council for funding towards highway improvements. Projects can include new or extended footpaths, traffic-calming measures, speed-reduction schemes, and other changes designed to improve road and pedestrian safety. Ramsey Town Council identifies potential projects and submits applications to Cambridgeshire County Council. Applications are assessed by the County Council and, if successful, funding is awarded towards the cost of the scheme. Under the current scheme, up to £25,000 can be awarded towards more complex projects, with applicants expected to contribute at least 10% of the overall cost. One recent LHI project was the extension of the footpath along Stocking Fen Road towards the industrial estate, improving pedestrian access for people travelling to and from work. The Council has also submitted an application for speed-reduction measures on the approach to Ramsey St Mary’s and is awaiting the outcome. Abbey College Road Safety Campaign Abbey College students are raising funds towards the £10,000 needed to help pay for speed reduction measures on Hollow Lane. Students have been campaigning, the school submitted an LHI bid, and speed cushions are planned. They would be grateful if you could spare the price of a coffee and scan the QR code.

items.title: Crews rush to 'deliberate' fire at former RAF base in Hunts village
items.content: Firefighters rushed to a "deliberate" fire at a derelict former RAF base in a Huntingdonshire village. Crews were called to the former RAF Upwood site on Ramsey Road near Bury on Saturday, November 21, at 3.31pm. The base opened in 1917 after a nearby farm was requisitioned for use as an emergency landing ground. Standing mostly derelict since 1994, the site has been the target of fly tipping and arson attacks for a number of years. However, there have been plans to redevelop areas into community facilities. Crews from Ramsey arrived to find a blaze on the ground floor of the derelict building and used a hose reel to extinguish it. They returned to the station by 4.10pm. A statement from Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service reads: "The cause of the fire is believed to be deliberate." Anyone with information should contact Cambridgeshire Police via their website, quoting incident 445 of November 21. Alternatively, call Crimestoppers on 0800 555111.

items.content: CIL - Community Infrastructure Levy What is CIL? Community Infrastructure Levy, commonly referred to as CIL, is money collected by Huntingdonshire District Council from certain new developments. The funding is then used to help provide or improve infrastructure needed as communities grow. The money collected is broadly divided into three areas: Up to 5% can be retained by Huntingdonshire District Council towards the administration and collection of CIL. 15% is normally allocated to the Town or Parish Council for the area where the development takes place. Once an adopted Neighbourhood Plan is in place, this increases to 25%. Most of the remaining funding is retained by Huntingdonshire District Council for larger strategic infrastructure projects across the district. Ramsey Town Council currently receives the 15% neighbourhood portion. Once the Ramsey Communities Neighbourhood Plan is adopted, this will increase to 25%, giving the Council a greater share of money from qualifying development to invest back into our communities. Current projects supported or earmarked through Ramsey Town Council’s CIL funding include: Improvements at The Moorings. Contributions towards Local Highways Improvement projects. Improvements to Newtown Road Play Park. Improvements to the public toilets. New benches at the skate park. CCTV at The Moorings and New Road. The Double Yellow Lines project. The Town Council is also considering future projects, including additional parking behind the doctor’s surgery at Mews Close. Local Highways Initiative Bid (LHI): what is an LHI? The Local Highway Improvement programme allows local councils and community organisations to apply to Cambridgeshire County Council for funding towards highway improvements. Projects can include new or extended footpaths, traffic-calming measures, speed-reduction schemes, and other changes designed to improve road and pedestrian safety. Ramsey Town Council identifies potential projects and submits applications to Cambridgeshire County Council. Applications are assessed by the County Council and, if successful, funding is awarded towards the cost of the scheme. Under the current scheme, up to £25,000 can be awarded towards more complex projects, with applicants expected to contribute at least 10% of the overall cost. One recent LHI project was the extension of the footpath along Stocking Fen Road towards the industrial estate, improving pedestrian access for people travelling to and from work. The Council has also submitted an application for speed-reduction measures on the approach to Ramsey St Mary’s and is awaiting the outcome. Abbey College Road Safety Campaign Abbey College students are raising funds towards the £10,000 needed to help pay for speed reduction measures on Hollow Lane. Students have been campaigning, the school submitted an LHI bid, and speed cushions are planned. They would be grateful if you could spare the price of a coffee and scan the QR code.

items.content: From a medieval bridge with its own chapel to a 55-arch causeway, Huntingdonshire is packed with unusual crossings. The district’s rivers, floodplains and Fenland waterways have shaped travel for centuries, leaving medieval crossings and Fen drainage bridges behind. Here are some of Huntingdonshire’s most striking bridges and where to find them. St Ives Bridge One of the county’s most extraordinary bridges spans the River Great Ouse at St Ives. The town’s first bridge was built of wood in 1107, before work began on a stone replacement in the early 15th century. The stone crossing was completed in 1425, and a chapel was added the following year. It is one of only three bridges in England with a chapel. The bridge also still bears the scars of the English Civil War. Parliamentary troops destroyed part of it to hinder Royalist forces, so a temporary drawbridge was installed. When the damaged section was rebuilt in 1716, it was given rounded arches instead of matching the pointed medieval ones, leaving a visible difference today. items.content: Message from the Mayor of Ramsey Hello everyone, I hope you’ve all had a wonderful summer. Personally, I can’t believe how quickly this year has flown by and that, as I write this, we’re already going into autumn. I want to use this column to recognise some amazing people - the Ramsey Town Council staff team, led by our Clerk, Lisa Renfree. They have had an incredibly busy summer, with lots of change and new initiatives to contend with as our Council grows and new Councillors come on board with the ambition to achieve and deliver more for our residents. They organised the Bands on the Green programme, delivered a family fun day at QEII Park with entertainment from the Blues Brothers and Queen tribute acts, produced and managed delivery of our newsletters to 5,000 homes, and got to grips with a new finance system. This was all on top of day-to- day customer service and administration, room bookings, council meetings and communications. They also stepped up to help coordinate meals and drinks for firefighters at Holme Fen during the recent wildfire, when the RRT Charity had to leave after a week. They do all of this professionally and with a smile. More often, however, they are facing abusive behaviour and, as a Council, this is something we will not tolerate. We have had to notify the police and use CCTV as evidence. Thankfully, this behaviour comes from a minority, and I know many of you appreciate the time our staff takes to assist you. So, from me and all fellow Councillors: thank you Lisa, Amanda, Kay, Alison, Quincy, Morgan and Paul - you are appreciated. Keep up the great work for our community. Thank you, Ramsey Parish community and beyond On behalf of Ramsey Town Council, we would like to thank everyone who supported the firefighters responding to the fire at Holme Fen. The response from local businesses, organisations and volunteers was incredible. Our thanks go to The Farmers Coffee Shop, Gorilla Pizza and Friar Tuck Fish & Chips for providing food and support; Ramsey Community Centre for opening its kitchen to prepare the large quantity of meals needed; The Admiral Wells for becoming a hub of activity, preparing meals and acting as a donation drop-off point; and Stevelyn & Creative Crafters for also providing a collection point, to name just a few. We would also like to thank the many volunteers who gave their time to prepare food and help wherever needed, as well as everyone who made donations. The JustGiving appeal raised an amazing £4,546.56. The Mayor also had the privilege of meeting The Duke of Gloucester during his visit to Holme Fen, where he saw the devastation caused by the fire and personally thanked firefighters, the owners of The Admiral Wells and local volunteers for their incredible efforts. The Lord-Lieutenant, Julie Spence, who accompanied him, spoke of how proud she was to see the community come together so quickly and effectively. Firefighters expressed their appreciation for every meal, drink and homemade cake provided during the response. Following the fire, a meeting of local community groups has been arranged for 1 October to discuss emergency planning and how the community can work together in response to future major incidents.
